name: Nikhil Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher from the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for a side. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior drilling assistant at a large mine. I help set up the rig, watch the pressure gauges, and fetch the right parts when the fitter calls for them. I finished secondary school and have been learning this work from the crew, often by asking the same question twice. I enjoy the sound when the bit finds a clean line in the rock. My partner Priya and I have two school-age children and a mortgage; my pay is normal for the job, but our savings would cover only a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drilling crew the little AI helpers have been useful for translating a manual into plain words, but we still check the rig ourselves. Last week I asked a tool about a pressure term, then made the fitter show me the actual gauge. A quick AI answer can't tell me what the drill rig's pressure gauge says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like trying new tools, though I'm still low on the crew list and need someone to check my work. If AI plateaus, the mortgage and the children's school costs still depend on my shifts. I sometimes worry my curiosity looks like confidence I haven't earned yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my drilling assistant shifts and ask the fitter to check my pressure readings. I'd put the next overtime payment into the emergency account rather than replace my phone. I'd use my AI tool after work to quiz myself on the manual, but never let it sign off a rig check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay about the technology. The money feels less settled; our account covers a few months, and a run of missed shifts would use it fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with that pressure term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I thought the manual was describing the return line, and the fitter showed me the feed line instead. We stood beside the panel until I could point to both without guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would notice if you used AI during a check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would, and he'd be right to object if I treated it as authority. I use it at home to learn the language, then I verify things on the rig.

say: I'd say AI can explain **manual terms**, but the crew must verify every rig reading.
I'd tell coworkers a faster explanation is not a **safe gauge reading**.
think: I enjoy new tools, but my **junior position** means my confidence can run ahead of my skill.
The mortgage and school costs still depend on **paid shifts**, even if AI stops advancing.
do: Keep assisting on the **drill rig** and ask the fitter to check pressure readings.
Put the next **overtime payment** into the emergency account instead of replacing my phone.
Use AI after work to quiz myself on the **manual**, without signing off checks.
feel: **Curious** about the tool, watchful about household money.
S0.quote: A quick AI answer can't tell me what the drill rig's pressure gauge says.
fieldNote: Nikhil experiments with AI daily but draws a firm **safety boundary** at physical readings on the rig.
His first financial move is to add the next **overtime payment** to a modest emergency fund.

steps.text: Keep assisting on drill rig shifts and verifying pressure readings
Put the next overtime payment into the emergency account
Use AI after work to practise drill manual terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use AI for buying bits and planning runs, provided the rig gets the right equipment on time. I'd volunteer to test the new job sheets against what we actually do at the drill. If a plan misses a safety step, I want it caught before the crew starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably learn the new screens faster than some people, but that's not the same as being secure. The office may need fewer planners, and a tighter drilling timetable could mean fewer people on my shift. Being the junior one makes me easy to leave off a roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for a trial of the digital job sheets, then compare five with our paper logs and show any misses. I'd keep drilling while that happens. If my shift count falls for a full month, I'd send applications to the two other mines within commuting distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel switched on, and I also feel exposed. The software could make me useful for a while without giving me any say over how many of us get hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which miss would make you stop a job sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing isolation step, straight away. I once watched a senior operator trace a line twice before touching it; a neat checklist must still name the right valve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a role running those screens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to help test them, yes, but I wouldn't leave paid rig shifts for a promise. My partner Priya and I have a mortgage, and software testing could disappear as quickly as it starts.

say: I'd offer to compare **digital job sheets** with the drill crew's real sequence.
I'd insist that AI planning still includes the correct **isolation step**.
think: Learning screens quickly might make me useful, but **junior shifts** could still disappear.
Fewer planners and tighter timetables might reduce **crew hours** before robots arrive.
do: Compare five **digital job sheets** with paper logs and flag missed steps.
Keep working paid **drill shifts** during the trial.
Apply to two nearby mines after a full month of **reduced shifts**.
feel: **Energised** by the trial and exposed to roster cuts.
S1.quote: The software could make me useful for a while without giving me any say over how many of us get hours.
fieldNote: Nikhil seeks a small **five-sheet trial** that can reveal concrete safety misses without giving up rig wages.
His public enthusiasm hides a specific fear about being **junior** when hours are allocated.

steps.text: Compare five digital job sheets with paper drill logs
Keep working paid drill shifts during the software trial
Apply to two nearby mines after one month of reduced shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full AGI in 2028 could handle the buying and planning before any robot touches the drill. I'd ask the mine to let current operators try the equipment it plans to bring in, rather than announce replacements from an office. Capable robots around 2031 would put our hands-on shifts directly in question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 45 when AGI arrives and 48 by the robot date. I'm quick to learn software, but that's not a guarantee they'll keep a junior worker to oversee an automated rig. Priya and I could cover a few months of expenses, not a long spell without pay while the children are still in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to observe the mine's remote control trials if they run any, and take a funded controls course if wages continue. I'd stay on paid drilling shifts while learning. In 2029, if our crew shrinks, I'd apply for remote equipment trainee jobs at nearby mines, knowing capable AGI could handle the controls later too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me want to move immediately, which isn't always wise. I can feel myself opening three course pages before I've asked whether any of them leads to paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask before taking a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the mine pays for it, whether classes fit my shifts, and how many actual trainee places follow. I'd show Priya the figures before touching our emergency money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you run a robot drill more safely than it runs itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. By 2031 the robot might make better choices than I do, especially on routine runs. I wouldn't bet our mortgage on a permanent human control seat.

say: I'd ask for operator access to **equipment trials** before robot drilling threatens shifts around 2031.
I'd explain that **planning and buying** change first with AGI in 2028.
think: At **48**, quick learning may not protect a junior driller from a shrinking crew.
Our few months of savings cannot fund a long **unpaid transition** with children at school.
do: Ask to observe **remote control trials** if the mine runs them.
Take a funded **controls course** only if wages continue, while keeping paid shifts.
Apply for nearby **remote equipment trainee** jobs in 2029 if the crew shrinks.
feel: **Driven** to act, but afraid of rushing into a poor course.
S2.quote: I wouldn't bet our mortgage on a permanent human control seat.
fieldNote: Nikhil's adaptability produces rapid **course research**, yet he checks funding and actual job places before committing.
He knows remote control work may also face **full AGI** and later robots, so he seeks options rather than safety claims.

steps.text: Observe remote control trials if the mine runs them
Take a funded controls course only if wages continue
Keep paid drilling shifts while learning controls
Apply for nearby remote equipment trainee jobs in 2029 if crews shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that five years gives us time to compare more than one route out of drilling. AGI in 2031 may reshape planning, and robots around 2034 may take the rig work itself. The mine should publish which jobs stay paid during the handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when the thinking work changes, I could have completed a controls certificate. By 51, when robots become capable, the children will be older but the mortgage could still be there. A certificate alone won't make me the person the mine keeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask next year for a funded controls place and also shadow the electrical team on approved shifts. I'd keep working the drill until I had a paid offer. In 2032, if planning changes reduce my hours, I'd apply for equipment diagnostics jobs at other mines as well as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one gives me enough room to compare actual work, not just course descriptions. I feel uneasy about losing the drill, but I can make one decision at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at electrical work as well as controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The controls course might be narrow, and I want to see how a fault is found on a real circuit. I'm still a learner on the rig, so I need to know whether I like the work before I train for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would diagnostics still exist after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps some paid roles would, but I can't know how many. AGI may do much of the diagnosis and robots may make the physical checks, so I'd apply early instead of treating it as a shelter.

say: I'd ask the mine to publish **paid handover jobs** before robot drilling arrives around 2034.
I'd say **AGI planning** changes by 2031, with hands-on rig work following later.
think: A **controls certificate** would widen my choices, but it would not secure a post at 51.
Older children ease some routines, while the **mortgage** may still need two incomes.
do: Request a funded **controls place** next year and shadow the electrical crew.
Continue paid **drill shifts** until a real offer arrives.
Apply for **equipment diagnostics** jobs in 2032 if my hours fall.
feel: **Uneasy**, yet able to compare two practical routes.
S3.quote: A certificate alone won't make me the person the mine keeps.
fieldNote: Nikhil uses the longer runway to test **controls and electrical work**, rather than committing to the first course.
He explicitly doubts that **diagnostics** will be protected after full AGI and capable robots.

steps.text: Request a funded controls place next year
Continue paid drill shifts until another job is offered
Apply for equipment diagnostics jobs in 2032 if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years is long enough to build a training ladder from the rig, not only a notice about the end. AGI in 2036 would change plans and technical records; capable robots around 2039 could do the drilling. We should be able to see the job openings each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at AGI and 56 by the robot date. Our children would be grown, but their independence and our mortgage balance are both unknown. I don't want to assume a pension or a safe oversight job; I want enough paid options to keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my rig shifts and ask for an electrical apprenticeship that pays wages, if the mine creates one. I'd use AI to study wiring diagrams with a qualified electrician checking my understanding, and put extra pay toward the mortgage. In 2037 I'd apply for paid plant maintenance roles once qualified, even though robots may later change that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This feels like a long project rather than a cliff. I would grieve the drill if the seat went, because I enjoy the moment when the bit settles into the rock. Ten years gives me time to become competent at something else, not just clever with an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the apprenticeship worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage during training, real workshop hours, and a qualification other employers recognise. I like learning fast, but I'm not going to call myself an electrician because a chatbot explained a diagram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine never offers it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the other mines about paid apprentice openings while I still had rig work. I could travel to a nearby site for a real place, but I wouldn't move the family on a guess.

say: I'd ask for a paid **training ladder** from the drill rig, with job openings published each year.
I'd explain that **AGI records** change in 2036 before robot drilling around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still need wages and cannot assume a pension or protected oversight role.
The children's needs and our **mortgage balance** will be different, but neither is settled today.
do: Keep paid **rig shifts** and seek a wage-paid electrical apprenticeship if offered.
Study **wiring diagrams** with AI and a qualified electrician checking my understanding.
Apply for paid **plant maintenance** posts in 2037 once qualified.
feel: **Sad** about the rig, but patient enough to build another skill.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to become competent at something else, not just clever with an app.
fieldNote: Nikhil is enthusiastic about AI learning but insists a **qualified electrician** verify practical understanding.
He sees the decade as time for **paid competence**, not a promise that maintenance survives capable robots.

steps.text: Keep paid drill rig shifts while seeking a wage-paid apprenticeship
Enter an electrical apprenticeship if it pays wages
Use AI with an electrician to study wiring diagrams
Apply for paid plant maintenance jobs in 2037 once qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The planning work might change before I'm fully skilled at the rig, and capable robots follow just three years later. A funded course with actual paid trainee places would help, along with time to try the equipment while I still earn a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the advice people get from these tools. I use AI every day, but the fitter still caught my mistake about the pressure line. A training plan needs a person who can say when the screen is wrong.

headlineQuote: A training plan needs a person who can say when the screen is wrong.
portrait: Nikhil is a **43-year-old junior miner** learning rig operations and pressure checks at a large mine.
He and Priya have two **school-age children**, a mortgage, and only a few months of savings.
He uses AI daily to learn, but checks its advice with a **qualified worker** at the rig.
He fears rapid robot drilling and seeks **paid training** and real vacancies while keeping his wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change the mine's planning before Nikhil masters the rig, with robot drilling around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course**, real paid trainee places, and equipment access while still earning would give him options.
